mathematicalReview.1: At least four vertices and at least three incident edges per vertex give 2E≥3V≥12; the displayed nondegenerate tetrahedron attains six edges.
mathematicalReview.2: A k-gonal prism has k lateral faces plus two bases, so k=n−2 and n≥5; the displayed pentagonal prism has the stated incidence counts.
mathematicalReview.3: Both adjacent side planes contain the unique perpendicular to the base through their common lower vertex; their intersection is the lateral-edge line. Parallel lateral edges establish a right prism for any base polygon.
mathematicalReview.4: The equivalence with a right prism is proved in both directions. The actual height KH is through interior points and is distinct from every lateral edge, avoiding coincident-line ambiguity.
mathematicalReview.5: The displayed right rhombic prism has all twelve edges of length 2, base angle 60 degrees, and a nonregular base; it is a valid counterexample.
mathematicalReview.6: For translation (1,0,2), the displayed A1H has length 2, lies inside the lateral parallelogram and is perpendicular to the base and AB. The lateral edge has length sqrt(5), so the prism is oblique.
mathematicalReview.7: In the exact right-triangular base and translation (1,0,2), the lateral direction is perpendicular only to AB, while the only vertical side plane is ACC1A1. The other two planes are excluded using the actual feet H and K, including external K. Skew-line perpendicularity is handled by parallel translation.
mathematicalReview.8: The two right prisms have base perimeters 3a/2 and 5a/2 and common height. Each new cut face is included in its own lateral surface, giving the ordered ratio 3:5.
mathematicalReview.9: Equal lateral-face edge lengths propagate around the apex. The height foot cannot be a base vertex, since an equilateral face would then have a right angle. Pythagoras puts all base vertices on one circle. Simplicity forces circular order; equal chords give minor angle theta, a major consecutive gap would make the total exceed 360 degrees, and the diameter case is excluded. Equal consecutive arcs establish a regular base and its center at the height foot. The actual five-sided model has equilateral lateral faces.
mathematicalReview.11: The actual convex quadrilateral has opposite-side extensions AB and CD meeting at external H. P above H makes exactly those two side-face planes vertical. The proof correctly permits a height foot outside the base.
mathematicalReview.12: The actual orthoscheme coordinates make ABC and ABD right at B, ACD and BCD right at C. The proof explicitly checks all four faces, including the fourth via the theorem of three perpendiculars.
mathematicalReview.13: The square base consumes 40 cm, so each equal lateral edge could be at most 6.5 cm. Nonzero height requires b>5sqrt(2), incompatible with that bound. The displayed pyramid is a valid illustrative shape and does not pretend that impossible 6.5 cm edges exist.
mathematicalReview.14: For the actual oblique prism, the cut plane A1BC leaves tetrahedron A1ABC and the quadrangular pyramid with apex A1 and base BCC1B1. Both complete face sets and the noncoplanarity of apex/base are explained. The argument uses only prism properties and applies to oblique as well as right prisms.
mathematicalReview.10-convex: A side-face plane is perpendicular to the base exactly when its base-side LINE contains the height foot. The actual square-base models realize exactly 0,1,2 such faces. Supporting-line classification establishes the upper bound of two for every convex base, including an external foot; plane membership is distinguished from membership in the bounded triangular face.
mathematicalReview.10-general: For every k≥3, choose k equally spaced rays from H and points at radii r and 2r. Alternating radial edges and connectors form a simple polygon: connector interiors lie in distinct sectors of angle 360/k<180 degrees, and radial segments lie on sector boundaries. Inner vertices are reflex, so the polygon is nonconvex. Exactly k radial side-lines pass through H; connector lines do not. Placing the apex above H gives exactly k perpendicular side faces. With the convex 0/1/2 examples, every nonnegative integer is possible when the base side count is not fixed. The actual k=3 coordinates realize the stated three faces and H is inside this revised base. Opposite radial faces for even k may be coplanar but remain distinct nonadjacent faces.
